clue.text: Support one needed at certain stages

definitions.meaning: something that holds up or bears weight
an object an actor handles on a theatre stage, needed only in certain productions

explanation.definitionFit: A buttress holding something up and a theatre object handled by actors share this one short word.

clue.text: Having fun, with stage production almost complete

parts.note: a drama put on in a theatre is a play

indicators.note: almost means the word is not quite finished, losing its final letter

parts.note: complete means full

explanation.surface: Someone enjoying themselves as their theatre show nears its finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts the last letter from FULL, leaving FUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone frolicking or joking is light-hearted and in high spirits.

clue.text: Dress coat perhaps made to officer's requirement

parts.note: to dress ranks is to put them in order, so dress means order
a coat of arms is heraldic arms, so coat is an example

explanation.surface: A formal dress coat tailored to an army officer's specification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made to' is a link. The answer is a drill command an officer gives, rifles to the side; 'Dress' is a drill word too, which helps hide the verb sense of arranging.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a parade-ground command barked by an officer, so it is something the officer requires of the troops.

clue.text: Providing a somewhat wordy description

parts.note: reads as long-winded prose, but means describing in the manner of a describing word, the part of speech that qualifies nouns

explanation.definitionFit: Grammar's qualifying words describe nouns, so anything acting like one supplies a description by way of a word.

clue.text: Put off covering study due for revision

parts.note: a den is a private study or retreat

indicators.note: revision suggests the letters of the word due are reworked into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A student delays the coursework they must revise, since it is due.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for revision' rearranges DUE to UDE. 'Put off' looks like postpone, but with 'covering' it means take the covering off.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip bare is to take off whatever was covering something.

clue.text: Informed verbally, after former spouse cracked up

indicators.note: after places the spoken word behind the former spouse

parts.note: EX is the usual word for a former husband or wife

indicators.note: verbally signals that the word for informed is heard spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: informed means told

explanation.surface: Someone, told the news by word of mouth after their ex did something, had a breakdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'verbally' turns TOLD into TOLLED, the same sound (as bells are tolled). 'cracked up' looks like breaking down but means praised, as in 'not all it's cracked up to be'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being much praised is being lauded highly; 'cracked up' is an idiom for that.

clue.text: Refreshing consolation from obscure American play

definitions.meaning: a cuppa offered with kindly comfort to someone upset
a 1953 Broadway drama by Robert Anderson, little remembered now

explanation.definitionFit: The British phrase means kindly comfort offered over a cuppa, and it is also the title of a Robert Anderson stage drama.

clue.text: Composer driven to distraction, forgetting finale

indicators.note: driven to distraction suggests frenzied disorder, so the letters are scrambled
forgetting its finale means the word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A musician pushed to despair forgets how the piece ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forgetting finale' drops the N of 'driven', and 'to distraction' scrambles DRIVE. 'finale' teases a musical ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi wrote operas such as Aida and La Traviata.

clue.text: Italian food provided, by the way — drop in!

indicators.note: in places the drooping word within the word for a way

parts.note: a lane is a way or narrow road
to sag is to drop or droop

explanation.surface: An invitation to drop by for some Italian cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drop in!' reads as a casual invitation to call round; split, the first word is the piece and 'in' the container signal. 'provided, by the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: This baked dish of flat pasta sheets layered with sauce comes from Italy.

clue.text: Start digging into how to innovate

definitions.meaning: to turn the first earth on a building site
to do something not done before

explanation.definitionFit: Literally, breaking soil to begin excavating; figuratively, pioneering something original.

clue.text: Great-sounding dog

parts.note: a dog found in something that sounds like 'great', a fireplace grate: a metal firedog supporting logs

explanation.definitionFit: A firedog is a metal support for logs standing in a fireplace grate.

clue.text: Saunter off for refreshments they provide

indicators.note: off suggests something gone wrong, so the letters of saunter are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone strolls away to get a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like going away but scrambles SAUNTER. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Large heated vessels at a canteen dispense hot drinks such as cuppas.

clue.text: Striker's plot — for future action?

parts.note: a striker in football is a forward
to plot is to be planning

explanation.surface: A footballer's scheme for what comes next in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' could be a worker on strike, but here it is a football attacker.
explanation.definitionFit: Arranging ahead is preparing in advance for what is to be done later.

clue.text: Sophia and zsa-zsa originally meeting zoologist

parts.note: Sophia Loren is the Italian film star

indicators.note: originally means only the opening letter of zsa-zsa is used

explanation.surface: Two film stars, Sophia and Zsa-Zsa, meet a scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meeting' and 'and' are links; 'zsa-zsa' would be Zsa Zsa Gabor, but only its first letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Konrad Lorenz was an Austrian scientist who studied animal behaviour, famous for imprinting in geese.

clue.text: See if lab's experiment is likely to work

indicators.note: an experiment tries things in new combinations, so the letters of see if lab are rearranged

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Checking whether a laboratory test is likely to succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'experiment' scrambles SEEIFLAB; the 's of 'lab's' adds no letter and 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something workable or practicable has a good chance of succeeding.

clue.text: Extra support for Indian-style cooking in us city

indicators.note: in a down entry a support goes underneath, so the extra word sits below the cooking word

parts.note: a balti is a curry dish cooked in a wok-like pan, popular in Britain
extra means more

explanation.surface: Someone asks for additional backing for curry restaurants in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: A balti is a British-Asian curry. In a down answer 'support for' puts MORE below BALTI.
explanation.definitionFit: Baltimore is a port city in Maryland in the United States.

clue.text: Refuse to give up, in a jam

definitions.meaning: to keep hold of and maintain

explanation.definitionFit: To keep and maintain something is to refuse to give it up; a fruit conserve is the noun sense.

clue.text: Investigating background of plan to steal from the post

parts.note: to case a place is to look it over before burgling it
a post is a job, one's work

explanation.surface: Detectives look into the background of a plot to rob mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post' suggests mail but means a job. 'of' and 'from' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Social workers and similar agencies study individual clients' histories and circumstances in detail.

clue.text: Ape seems to act tigerishly?

definitions.meaning: acting like a tiger is mimicking a big feline, read as two words

explanation.definitionFit: A mimic apes others, and mimicking a tiger is literally imitating a feline.

clue.text: Charm in the form of a cross, first of talismans

parts.note: a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey

indicators.note: first of means just the opening letter of talismans

explanation.surface: A lucky charm shaped like a crucifix, the first among talismans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' suggests a crucifix but means a hybrid animal. 'in the form of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A trinket worn to ward off evil is a lucky talisman.

clue.text: One produces leather, in attempt to dress a woman

indicators.note: dressing someone clothes them, so the attempt word wraps around the woman

parts.note: an attempt is a try
Anne is a woman's name

explanation.surface: Someone tries to put clothes on a woman, using leather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to dress' means to clothe, so the attempt goes round the woman like a garment. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A works where hides are cured into leather is a place that produces it.

clue.text: Example of road-rage — it's unreal

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway, written with I for 1
taken as written

explanation.surface: A driver's road-rage outburst is dismissed as unreal.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; crosswords often write it as MI.
explanation.definitionFit: An optical illusion, such as water seen on a hot road, is something that is not real.

clue.text: Thieving from the enemy?

parts.note: the enemy is time, and the proverb calls putting things off the thief of time

explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says delay is the thief of time, and time is the old enemy, so habitual delaying robs it.

clue.text: European awards at first carrying too much weight

indicators.note: at first puts the awards word before the European letter

parts.note: OBEs are British honours, Officers of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: European honours given out early on to someone overweight.
explanation.walkthrough: An OBE is a British honour. 'at first' means the awards come first, then E.
explanation.definitionFit: Being very fat means carrying much more weight than is healthy.

clue.text: Vet may be told to put things in black and white, perhaps

definitions.text: put things in black and white, perhaps

indicators.note: told means spoken aloud, so the word for one who vets is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to vet is to check, so one who vets is a checker

explanation.surface: A vet might be instructed to record things in writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be told' is the sound signal. To mark in a pattern of squares, as on a chessboard, is to colour in black and white; the 'perhaps' allows other colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Marking a surface with alternating squares, as on a draughtboard, often uses black and white.

clue.text: Silly hat only seen in Irish town

indicators.note: silly suggests jumbled nonsense, so the letters of hat are rearranged

parts.note: only means lone, single

explanation.surface: A ridiculous hat spotted on a single occasion in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' scrambles HAT to ATH; 'seen in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Athlone is a town on the River Shannon in the middle of Ireland.

clue.text: Delete slur involving "wimp" for aggressive twin

indicators.note: involving means the scrambled letters surround the word for a wimp
a slur is a blurred mangling, so the letters of delete are rearranged

parts.note: a weed is a feeble weakling

explanation.surface: Someone told to delete an insult containing the word wimp aimed at a combative sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slur' rearranges the clue's first word into TLEDEE, and 'involving' wraps that around the wimp after its T. In Lewis Carroll the twins agree to fight. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In Through the Looking-Glass this brother agrees to do battle with his identical sibling over a rattle.

clue.text: Anyone would have to refuse to do this

definitions.text: Anyone would have to refuse to do this

parts.words: Anyone would have to refuse to do this
parts.note: if told to do this, obeying would mean failing, so the only way to comply is to refuse

explanation.definitionFit: To flout an order is to refuse it, so carrying out an instruction to flout means refusing.
